To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the CBF responses to CO2 during hypoxia or normoxia are best characterized as two-component responses with a breakpoint in PETCO2 at approximately 43 and 49 mmHg, respectively, and the two-component responses to CO2 are related to the two-component responses in VE.

CBF increased in two distinct linear phases with increasing PCO2 during both hypoxic (50 mmH g) and hyperoxic (200 mmH g) rebreathing, but the breakpoint separating these phases was likely not due solely to PCO2, since PETCO 2 increased linearly, nor to perfusion pressure, as MAP also increased linearly.
the two components in the CBF response to PCO2 during hypoxia and hyperoxia are not explained by changes in PCO2 or MAP, but they may be related to ventilation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of hyperoxia and hypoxia on CBF.
the effects of oxygen and carbon dioxide on CBF and VE during hypoxia and hyperoxia.
how the brain responds to changes in oxygen (O2) and carbon dioxide (CO2).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CBF is regulated by a two-component system, with the first component being the response to the change in PCO2 and the second being the response to changes in VE.
CBF responses to CO2 during hypoxia and hyperoxia are similar to those during normoxia, with the exception of the two-component response to CO2.
the two-component CBF response to CO2 is not due to PCo2 per se, but is due to the neural linkage between CBF and ventilation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the two-component CBF response to CO2 is maintained during hyperoxia and hypoxia and is not due to changes in PETCO2 or perfusion, but may be related to changes in VE.
the CBF response to CO2 is not linear and that the CBF and VE responses to CO2 are similar and may be regulated by the same neural mechanism.
the cerebral circulation is sensitive to changes in CO2 during both hyperoxia and hypoxia.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the CBF response to CO2 in humans is not linear.

the cerebral circulation exhibits a two-component response to changes in PCO2 during hypoxia and hyperoxia, and that the transition between the two components occurs at the same PCO2 during both hyperoxic and hypoxic breathing.
the CBF response to CO2 during hypoxia and hyperoxia is biphasic and that the two components of the response are regulated by a common mechanism.
